hero.subtitle: Copper Tripeptide-1
hero.short_summary: GHK-Cu is the copper(II) complex of glycyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine, the tripeptide Loren Pickart and Marvin Thaler first described in human serum in 1973. Ingredient suppliers list it as Copper Tripeptide-1, and drug-development literature calls it prezatide copper. Veracue supplies it as a research material for laboratory work. It carries a far larger published literature than most copper peptides, though almost all of it sits in cell culture and animal models, and the human data that does exist comes from topical cosmetic formulations rather than from research powder.

sections.heading: Overview
body: GHK-Cu pairs a three-amino-acid peptide with a single copper(II) ion. The peptide is glycine, histidine and lysine in that order, which is where the initials come from. Copper binds through nitrogen donors from the glycine terminus and the histidine side chain, and the peptide gives up amide protons as the metal locks in.

The compound reached the literature by accident. In 1973 Loren Pickart and Marvin Thaler reported in Nature New Biology that a small fraction of human serum kept liver cells alive in culture longer than expected. The active fraction turned out to be this tripeptide. Seven years later a Nature paper from Pickart and colleagues proposed that the peptide works largely by shuttling copper into cells, which is still the framing most mechanistic work starts from.

Two other names follow GHK-Cu around. Cosmetic ingredient lists call it Copper Tripeptide-1. Older drug-development records call the peptide prezatide and the complex prezatide copper. All three point at the same chemistry, but they belong to different regulatory worlds, and a cosmetic safety conclusion does not carry over to a research powder.

sections.heading: Intended Use
body: This material is offered for in vitro and laboratory research. Typical contexts include fibroblast and keratinocyte culture, extracellular matrix and wound-model work, copper coordination chemistry, and analytical method development.

It is not a drug, cosmetic, supplement or food, and it is not intended for administration to humans or animals. Nothing on this page provides dosing, application, reconstitution for administration, or treatment information, and none of it should be read that way.

sections.heading: Molecular Identity and Why the Numbers Disagree
body: Look up the molecular weight of GHK-Cu and you will find at least five different numbers. They are not all errors. Most of them describe genuinely different species, and a couple of the figures circulating on supplier pages are arithmetic that does not hold up.
The table below sets each representation against its formula so a researcher can match a catalogue value or a COA entry to the species it actually describes.
rows: Neutral 1:1 Cu(II) complex, two protons displaced
CAS 89030-95-5; the formula CosIng lists for Copper Tripeptide-1; the value most research suppliers quote
1:1 Cu complex written as a cation
CAS 130120-57-9; DrugBank DBSALT002420; sold as Copper Tripeptide-1 (2:1, HOAc)
post_table_body: Two corrections are worth making plainly, because both circulate widely.

First, a number of pages pair the formula C14H22CuN6O4 with a weight near 403.9 g/mol. That formula sums to 401.91. The 402.92 figure belongs to the cationic form PubChem draws, which carries one more hydrogen. A difference of one proton is small, but if a report says the two are the same thing, it was not checked.

Second, the acetate form is often listed around 462 to 467 g/mol, as though it were a 1:1 complex with one acetate attached. The registered substance behind CAS 130120-57-9 is not that. DrugBank records prezatide copper acetate as two peptide units, one copper and two acetates, averaging 860.39 g/mol. Some suppliers do sell a 1:1 mono-acetate, which is a different material again.

For a research powder the practical question is narrow. Which species did the vendor synthesise, and which species did the identity test match against? A COA that reports a mass without naming the form leaves that unanswered.

sections.heading: GHK and GHK-Cu Are Not Interchangeable
body: Plenty of sources use GHK and GHK-Cu as if they were one compound. They are not. GHK is the bare tripeptide, 340.38 g/mol, CAS 49557-75-7, a white peptide solid. GHK-Cu is the copper complex, roughly 402 g/mol depending on how the form is written, CAS 89030-95-5, and copper gives it colour.

The distinction has teeth in the literature. Several influential findings were produced with the free peptide rather than the complex. The 2012 Genome Medicine analysis that reported reversal of an emphysema-related gene signature used GHK, not GHK-Cu. Reviews that fold both into one story quietly blur which molecule was in the flask.

It also matters for what arrives in the vial. If a vendor labels a product GHK-Cu but the identity result matches 340 g/mol, the material is the free peptide and the copper is either absent or unaccounted for.

sections.heading: What Copper Tripeptide-1 Means, and What It Does Not
body: Copper Tripeptide-1 is the cosmetic ingredient name for GHK-Cu. It sits in the EU CosIng database under reference 55687 against CAS 89030-95-5 and the formula C14H22CuN6O4. Copper Tripeptide-3 is the parallel name for AHK-Cu, which is why the two get mixed up on supplier pages.

In 2018 the Cosmetic Ingredient Review Expert Panel assessed Tripeptide-1, Copper Tripeptide-1 and related derivatives and concluded they are safe in the present practices of use and concentration in cosmetics. That conclusion is worth reading closely. The Panel anchored it to typical use concentrations below 10 ppm in finished cosmetic products.

So the CIR conclusion says something about a fraction of a percent of peptide in a lotion. It says nothing about a vial of lyophilized powder, nothing about any other route, and nothing about biological activity. It is a cosmetic-ingredient finding, and it should not be recycled as a safety statement for research material.

sections.heading: What the GHK-Cu Research Actually Shows
body: GHK-Cu has an unusually deep literature for a tripeptide, stretching back five decades. The depth is real. The evidence tier is narrower than most product pages imply.

The core findings come from cultured human fibroblasts. Maquart and colleagues reported in FEBS Letters in 1988 that GHK-Cu stimulated collagen synthesis in fibroblast culture. Work through the 1990s and 2000s extended that to glycosaminoglycans and small proteoglycans in wounded skin, and to matrix metalloproteinase and TIMP expression. Kang and colleagues reported changes in integrin expression and p63 positivity in keratinocytes in 2009.

The strongest animal data is the 1993 Journal of Clinical Investigation study from Maquart's group, which found increased connective tissue accumulation in rat experimental wounds after GHK-Cu treatment. That is a living system, but it is a rat wound, not a person.

Human data exists and is thinner than its citation count suggests. The study nearly every page leans on is Leyden and colleagues, presented at the American Academy of Dermatology annual meeting in February 2002: a facial cream containing copper peptide, assessed over 12 weeks. It is a conference abstract for a cosmetic formulation, not a full peer-reviewed trial report of the compound itself. A 2016 Journal of Aging Science paper from Badenhorst and colleagues looked at MMP and TIMP expression alongside facial wrinkle parameters. Both tested finished topical products.

One more thing a careful reader should know. A large share of the review literature, including the widely cited 2018 International Journal of Molecular Sciences paper, comes from Loren Pickart and Anna Margolina at Skin Biology, a company that sells copper peptide products. The primary research they summarise is real. The framing carries a commercial interest that is rarely disclosed when those reviews get cited.

sections.heading: The Hair Claims Need Untangling
body: Search interest in GHK-Cu and hair is enormous, and the content answering it is unusually unreliable. Three separate evidence streams get merged into one.

The first is genuine GHK-Cu work, which is thin on follicle endpoints. Uno and Kurata's 1993 Journal of Investigative Dermatology supplement reviewed chemical agents and peptides affecting hair growth in animal models, and copper peptide work sits inside that tradition.

The second stream is AHK-Cu, not GHK-Cu. The 2007 Archives of Pharmacal Research study by Pyo and colleagues, which tested isolated human scalp follicles and cultured dermal papilla cells, used AHK-Cu. Its findings, including the Bcl-2 to Bax ratio shift and reduced cleaved caspase-3, are routinely reattributed to GHK-Cu online. They are not GHK-Cu findings.
The third stream is general copper-peptide literature, which gets narrated as though every result applies to every copper peptide.

One specific citation is worth flagging. Several pages attribute a Wnt and beta-catenin activation finding in human dermal papilla cells to a 2018 Scientific Reports article. We could not locate that paper. Until a primary source turns up, treat that claim as unverified rather than established.

sections.heading: GHK-Cu Compared With AHK-Cu
body: Both are copper(II) complexes of a tripeptide ending in histidine and lysine. The only structural difference is the first residue: glycine in GHK-Cu, alanine in AHK-Cu. That single change is enough to give them separate CAS numbers, separate INCI names and very different research histories.

No controlled study comparing the two head to head was identified. Neither can be called stronger, better or more effective on the published record. What can be said is that they have been studied in different models, for different questions, at very different volumes.

sections.heading: Reading a GHK-Cu Certificate of Analysis
body: A purity percentage answers one question out of six. A useful GHK-Cu COA should let you confirm what the material is, which form it is, how pure it is by a named method, how much peptide is actually in the vial, whether copper is present in the expected ratio, and that the report belongs to the lot in your hand.

Copper complexes make the identity question sharper than it is for ordinary peptides. Because the free peptide, the neutral complex, the cationic form and the acetate salt all carry different masses, an identity result is only interpretable if the report states which species it was matched against.

sections.heading: HPLC and LC-MS Answer Different Questions
body: These two methods get quoted together so often that they start to read like one test. They are not, and they fail in different directions.

HPLC separates what is in the sample and reports how much of the detected signal sits under the main peak. It is a purity measure. It cannot tell you that the main peak is the molecule you wanted. A clean chromatogram of the wrong compound still looks clean.

Mass spectrometry answers the identity question by measuring mass. It tells you whether the species present matches an expected mass, which is exactly what a copper complex needs, since the metal changes the number. It does not tell you what fraction of the vial that species represents.
rows: Chromatographic purity under stated conditions; presence of related substances
Whether the main peak is the intended molecule; how much peptide is in the vial
Whether an observed mass matches the expected species, including the copper-bound form
Safety, biological activity, endotoxin status or suitability for any use in a living system

faqs.a: GHK-Cu is the copper(II) complex of the tripeptide glycyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine, first described in human serum by Pickart and Thaler in 1973. It is supplied here as a laboratory research material.

faqs.q: Is GHK the same as GHK-Cu?
faqs.a: No. GHK is the free tripeptide, C14H24N6O4, 340.38 g/mol, CAS 49557-75-7. GHK-Cu is the copper complex, CAS 89030-95-5, around 402 g/mol depending on the form. Several well-known studies used the free peptide rather than the complex, so the distinction changes which findings apply.

faqs.q: Is GHK-Cu the same as Copper Tripeptide-1?
faqs.a: Yes, chemically. Copper Tripeptide-1 is the cosmetic ingredient name, listed in CosIng under reference 55687 against CAS 89030-95-5. The name belongs to cosmetic formulation, not to research material, and a cosmetic safety assessment does not carry over to a research powder.

faqs.q: What is the sequence of GHK-Cu?
faqs.a: Glycine, histidine, lysine, in that order, with a copper(II) ion bound through nitrogen donors from the glycine terminus and the histidine side chain.

faqs.q: Why do sources list different molecular weights for GHK-Cu?
faqs.a: Because they describe different species. The free peptide is 340.38. The neutral 1:1 copper complex, C14H22CuN6O4, is 401.91. PubChem's cationic depiction, C14H23CuN6O4+, is 402.92. A 2:1 adduct is 744.31, and prezatide copper acetate, CAS 130120-57-9, is 860.39. A value near 403.9 paired with the formula C14H22CuN6O4 is an arithmetic error; that formula sums to 401.91.

faqs.q: What is the CAS number for GHK-Cu?
faqs.a: 89030-95-5 for the copper complex. The free peptide GHK is 49557-75-7, and prezatide copper acetate is 130120-57-9. Because suppliers attach these numbers to different forms, confirm which form a given lot represents.

Prezatide is the drug-development name for the GHK peptide, and prezatide copper is the copper complex under that nomenclature. It appears in regulatory and pharmaceutical registries, including older records under names such as PC-1020 and Iamin. It refers to the same chemistry as GHK-Cu.

faqs.q: What does the human evidence for GHK-Cu show?
faqs.a: The human evidence comes from topical cosmetic formulations, not from research powder. The most-cited study, Leyden and colleagues at the 2002 American Academy of Dermatology meeting, assessed a copper peptide facial cream over 12 weeks and was presented as a conference abstract. A 2016 Journal of Aging Science paper looked at MMP and TIMP expression alongside wrinkle parameters. Neither tested the raw compound.

faqs.q: Is GHK-Cu proven to grow hair?
faqs.a: No. No human randomised trial with hair endpoints was identified. Much of the follicle research attributed to GHK-Cu online actually belongs to AHK-Cu, particularly the 2007 Pyo study on isolated human scalp follicles and dermal papilla cells.

faqs.q: What is the difference between GHK-Cu and AHK-Cu?
faqs.a: One amino acid. GHK-Cu starts with glycine, AHK-Cu with alanine. GHK-Cu is a native human plasma peptide with a large literature across fibroblast, wound and topical studies. AHK-Cu's direct evidence centres on a single 2007 hair-follicle paper. No head-to-head study was identified, so neither can be called superior.

faqs.q: What should a GHK-Cu Certificate of Analysis include?
faqs.a: Lot number matching the vial, a named purity method with its conditions, an identity result stating the expected mass, the observed mass and the species matched, the molecular form the result refers to, copper accounting, net peptide content where measured, and the testing laboratory and date.

faqs.q: Does high HPLC purity mean GHK-Cu is safe or biologically active?
faqs.a: No. HPLC purity describes the share of detected signal under the main peak in a single chromatographic run. It says nothing about identity, net peptide content, sterility, endotoxin status, biological activity or suitability for use in any living system.

faqs.q: What does research use only mean for this product?
faqs.a: It means the material is manufactured, labelled and supplied for in vitro and laboratory research only. It is not for human or veterinary use, not for ingestion, injection or any form of administration, and not for compounding.
